projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Elizabeth Jane Wachs was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: And it is January 13th, 2003, and we are at North Lincoln County Historical Museum in Lincoln City, Oregon, and I am interviewing Elizabeth Jane Wachs. Her maiden name is Taggeter. (ph) She lives at [address redacted], in Lincoln City, and she is 80 years old. Is that right?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: As of end of last year, yeah.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: And how do you pronounce the town in Nebraska where you were born?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Orleans.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Orleans?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: And my name is Libby Durbin, and I am the educator here. Okay, Betty. Do you want to tell me just a little bit about your early life in Nebraska and then move up to the War years and how you got from there to California?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Okay. Well, I was born and raised in the eastern part of the straight Nebraska in Orleans. And then, when I was in about the second or third grade, we moved out to Gering, which is in the panhandle of Nebraska right next to Scottsbluff, which was on the Oregon Trail. And then, I graduated from high school in '39, and then, I worked for doctors and a dentist and then moved to California because I had never been in a factory, and we had family friends that lived in Burbank, California, and I went out and got a job at Lockheed Aircraft, which was also known as Vega 2. They had different areas where they had aircraft plants.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Was that in '39?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: No. That was about in '42 because after I got out high school.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: So the War had already started?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: I beg your pardon?

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: The War had already started?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Is that why you went out there?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yeah, I wanted to help.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Help with that.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Help win the War.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: So you had to take a test at Lockheed, and I could remember later on my husband Sydney, which was my husband then, told me that he asked how I did because you had to take some classes on how to use drills and rivet guns, and I said oh, I handled it just like an egg beater. So anyway, that's what I did for a while. That was standing on cement floors, and it was hard work, but it was interesting, and I worked on the B7 cowlings.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Tell me exactly what you did.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Well, on the cowlings, you used the drill to put the holes in the cowling, and then, you would add a piece on to it and use a rivet gun and what they called a buck bar; that the buck bar was behind the other side of the metal, and you used the rivet gun on the one side. So they had two people working together, one on one side of the metal and the other on the other side. So it was usually a man and usually seemed to pair up men and women, and there were a lot women working there. I think that's how things started with women going back to work.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: And so --

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: So how did you feel about --

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: So many people had families in the Service, and they wanted to get this War over with. And there is one thing, I met Sydney, he was a tool designer, and he eventually felt that he would like to go into the Service. So he passed to become an ensign officer, and Lockheed would not release him. So he kept on working until then the draft, they got to where they really needed more men, and they started after the aircraft plants making them release some of the men. So then, he went in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Were you married at that time?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: No, no. We got married when he was in Service, and it was really funny, he had always told me he wanted to take me up to Carmel, California, and when he got through with boot camp, he was a radio technician with the Navy, for the Navy, and they told him he had five different places to choose to where he could go to, to do his regular work. And so one of them was right outside Carmel, California. So little did we know that the Navy made it upon for us to have our honeymoon or get married there, and they had a beautiful base, Monterey, California, which is right next to Carmel, and they took over a beautiful, beautiful hotel called Delmar. And it was just lovely. And I remember we had Christmas in there. I went up Christmas, I got the C coupons from different people that worked at Lockheed, and so I went up there to --

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Now, explain what that is for somebody that wouldn't know.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: The C coupons.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Oh, those were gas coupons. We were only allowed so many gallons a month, and we were given the coupons, and they were called C coupons. So several people in the plant got together and gave me enough coupons that I could drive up there and take his mother, and we went up the there for Christmas. But before that, we had gotten married up there.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: What was a wedding like? Was it any different than it would have been if there hadn't been a War on?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Well, yes, because we had to get married up there, and we had a Navy chaplain that had a nice little chapel, and we were married by the Navy chaplain, and the -- all the people that were really at the wedding were Syd's Service people, the Navy men and my inlaws or his parents and the best man and the bridesmaid, the maid of honor came up there for the wedding. And so we had our honeymoon there in Carmel, and then, I eventually had to go back down to go to work.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: How much time did you have?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: And then, I did work -- I came up there and stayed with Syd until he was through there, and then, he was sent to Corpus Christi, Texas, and another Service man, a Navy man and his wife and their little three-year old girl, we drove all the way to Corpus Christi, Texas, from Carmel, California.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Wasn't as easy as it is today.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: No, it isn't. And it was -- we were two women with a two year-old child, and en route she got chicken pox. That was very interesting, and so when we would stay at a hotel, I would go in and get the room, and then I'd go back out to get Olivia and her little daughter, and we would have her wrapped up in a blanket because we didn't want them to see that she had chicken pox. So we probably spread chicken pox from here to Corpus Christi, I mean, from Carmel, California, to Corpus Christi, Texas. So any then --

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: What kind of a car did you have?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: It was a Chevy. I don't know the year now, but it was new. It was my husband's, and again, the people gave us enough stamps to help us get down to Texas. And so then, let's see, what else happened? That's --

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Well, let's go back to Lockheed. You worked there from 1943 to 1946?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yeah. We were married in '45. St. Patrick's Day went to Carmel, so my dates, I know the marriage, the day we got married, I remember that, and then, we had a big dinner at the hotel, all the Service men and the people that were involved in the wedding and my in-laws and an uncle of (sets). So my family was all back in Grasban (ph). During that time, it was (?too far to travel so far?).

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Well, they didn't meet Syd until --

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: They met him -- let's see. When he came home from boot camp, we did take a trip back to Nebraska, and I think that was one of the funniest things because we had to take a train, and he was, you know, on leave.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Huh-huh.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Took a train. And it was a coal passenger car, and it was right at the center of the car, and over on the right side were the windows. So the right side of us was freezing because it was winter. The left side was roasting from the coal and every time the conductor came through, he would throw another shovel of coal on the fire, and we about roasted. That was quite a trip. But anyway there was one thing I wanted to say about my husband, too. When he was at Lockheed, he worked with a lot people, and he was the vice president of the union in those days.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: What was the union?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: The union was for aeronautical people, and I can't remember, you know, the exact name of it. But anyway he was the vice president. Well, the president was gone most of the time of the union back in Washington, D.C. as far as the people that worked in the factories. What was interesting was when the union -- they would not allow the blacks in the union.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Were there a lot of black people that worked at Lockheed?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yes. There were some. I wouldn't say a lot, but there were quite a few. And he was very unhappy that they were not allowed to be in the union. He really, really was unhappy about that. And so he felt they had sons and daughters, brothers in the Service, and but, yet, they were working for the Government, but they couldn't be put in the union. So he fought for the blacks to be able to join the union. He thought that was only fair.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Who did he have to the fight about that?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: The other members of the union. There was some there were anti, and it was a scary time because they planted communist literature in his mailbox, and you know, he was still living at home when he was working at Lockheed. And so -- I mean, with his parents -- so it was scary. They even threw a rock through the window of his parents' home.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Right. So it was sad and scary and also made you angry to think that these people did not want blacks to join the union, and they were sending and losing their family, too, during the War.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: So was he successful?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yes. He was successful. It was mighty hard, but -- and it was like I said, it was scary. And they tried their best to get him out of the union.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Well, what was his full name, and when was he born?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: He was born in 1918, and his name was Sydney Wachs, W-a-c-h-s, and he was born and raised in New York. He came to California in ninth -- 1938 because he graduated from Hollywood High in 1939, and then, he went on to UCLA and graduated from UCLA in -- let's see. What year was that? 1939. So that was the same year I graduated from high school he graduated from UCLA, four years difference.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: What did he major in.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: He majored in math and psychology.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: That's an interesting difference.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. He had a hard time after he got out of college trying to find a job. But then, when he went to work for Lockheed because he was so good in math and drafting and designing, so that worked out okay for him. But then, when he got out of the Service, he went back to Lockheed and worked there for about a year. And of course, there were so many people coming back from the War to their jobs that they had before they had more employees than they really needed. So they started cutting back, and I remember he was on swing shift, and so that was a different way of life for us, but eventually, he started looking for other work. And he saw an ad for probation work with the LA County. And so he passed that test and went to work and worked there for 32 years and became the -- well, he was the one that started the work furlough program for LA County, for when people are on probation, and then, they need to still support their family, and it kept them from using the welfare money. So what they did was, they put them on -- it had to be okay for their -- the employer; that they could work and then go to jail on the weekends. And that way they still had an income for the family and weren't on welfare. So he started that program in LA County, and he worked in juvenile traffic division. He was in charge of that and the first one, the administrator of that department. So anyway that's --

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Well, now, I want to go back to your job at Lockheed. This tripod doesn't work. I will take that out.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: So when did that term "Rosie the Riveter" come along because you were one?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: I don't remember just when that happened, and then, they had be big poster. Rosie the Riveter were quite predominant in different areas.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: So were you proud of your role?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Oh, sure, because I was out there to help with the War. It was better than going out on the lines ___+. That wouldn't be my forte. That's what happened.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Who trained you?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Well, you got a class.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: And then, you worked -- they put you to work with somebody that had been doing that type of work what it was. And I ended up, after a while it got kind of monotonous and tiring and standing and pushing. So I ended up working in the receiving office after about a year doing that other work __+.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: And what did you do there?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: -- in the office.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Wrote up the -- we would get materials in, and then, we would have to be sure that it was proper, and we had all the Government forms, you know, and we had to type in everything, the work order, where it came from, what job it was to be used on, which planes. Well, they had so many different codes that you had to put on these forms, and I was -- I did a lot of typing on that job.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Did you belong to the union?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yes. Yes, I did.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Were there any special rules at Lockheed as far as, you know, anything about confidentiality and all that?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yes. You had to keep still. You couldn't say too much about what you had done or how many cowlings were done back during the day. We also had a canteen on what was part of the parking lot. They had a lot of entertainment, and I had done a lot music solo when I was in high school. I was in a girl's sextet, next (?octet,) and I did solo work. And so I used to do some solo work, and I laugh because I wanted to go on that, and one of the fellows had a connection with the music industry from Hollywood, and that's where we lived, in Hollywood, but we drove to Burbank at the plant. And so I was going to go back to taking some more music. And this fellow tried to get me to do that and maybe get a job with a band, but Syd didn't think too much of that.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Was there any -- did you develop friendships during your type at Lockheed?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Are you still in touch --

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: That was my matron of honor --

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: -- the one that I used to work with. And then, eventually, people moved around so much during the War, and you don't always keep contact, but I still am in contact with people that we knew when he was stationed in Corpus Christi, Texas.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Uh-huh. I still get Christmas cards and keep in contact with several of those people because they were couples. We went through the same thing together, had a lot fun together when we were down in Corpus Christi. I worked there for the Government.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Did you? What did you do there?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: I worked in the department where they gave the ensigns their orders. I would type up and issue their orders as to where their next place they were to present to.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Uh-huh. Well, what happened in 1946 when the War was over, and you stopped working at Lockheed?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Well, then, Syd and I -- let's say I had -- better turn that off a minute. (Pause.)

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Now I got it on.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Okay. After he was through at Corpus Christi, then we were sent to San Leandro, and I think it was Camp Shoemaker, that's where he got his discharge papers. Then we went back to LA, and that's when he went to work for Lockheed and then went back to the probation department and got a job with the probation department.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: I skipped around here.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: So did you keep on working?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: For a little while, and then I got pregnant so I had a little girl born in 1946 November around Thanksgiving time.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Did you work at any other time in your life?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Oh, yes, __ yeah, I had a second daughter. The first one was named Sandra Lou, and we had another one, Germaine Rae, and they were almost three years apart, and when they were in upper grade school, I got a part-time job with La Canada where we lived, La Canada, California. It is a suburb of LA. And I ended up by working for the water district there and helped with the water assessment and the bill. And then, after awhile, I went to work with the Camp Fire Girls, a professional. I had been a leader with the Camp Fire Girls, and then, one daughter was in Camp Fire. The other one was in Scouts. That was -- they were competing in the same type of organization, and then, I eventually -- when they got older, I got a job with the state of California, and I worked in the disability insurance office.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Well, you've worked your whole life.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: So that's it.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: I have got two granddaughters and two great granddaughters.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Oh, boy.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: No boys.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: So tell me, how did you entertain yourself when you weren't working at Lockheed?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Oh, during the War?

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: What did you and Syd do. He was in the Navy by then.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Well, Syd had a lot of hobbies. He was an avid reader, and he also got into photography. He loved to take pictures. The girls used to get a little annoyed with their dad because he would take forever to get everything set, and they would say "dad, hurry up." And so you mean what did we do?

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: What did you do when you were both working at Lockheed? Before you got married, what kind of entertainment, what was there to do when you weren't at work?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Well, we lived in Hollywood, California. I mean, I had an apartment. I mean, he lived in Hollywood. I lived in Burbank.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: And so on our dates, we went to a lot of movies. And then, there was Hollywood Bowl. It was an interesting place --

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Did you see any of the stars?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Can you remember --

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: I can't remember who they all were at this time. No, I can't right now.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Did you ever see anybody on the street?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yes. I think I remember seeing Bing Crosby one time in his car. Oh, and the place my husband lived was close to NBC and CBS and Lux Radio Theater. So that was wonderful. We could go up there, and it was all free. And that was the best entertainment because we saw a lot of the radio programs. We saw, oh, Bob hope and Merv Griffin got a lot these people started, and I was trying to think of some of the other people that we saw there. Well, there was all kinds programs there, Lux Radio Theater.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: And it was really a nice place to be at that time because the entertainment was free. You could go there.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: See them putting on the show?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: The Blackouts, I can't remember the fellow that had the Blackouts. And he was a comedian and had some -- a lot stars on. I can't remember the name, but I remember I saw Walter Pidgeon on, and that was wonderful. Then, one day when we had our girls we went to the beach, and coming back we stopped at an ice cream parlor, and I stayed in the car. Well, Syd took the girls in to get some ice cream, and I heard this voice that I just -- oh, I thought, oh, that has got to be Gregory Peck, and I looked out the window, and here was Gregory Peck walking right by the car with a little girl on the inside of him. But his voice was so easy to know that that had to be him. Nobody else had a voice like him. So that was kind of an exciting moment that day. I couldn't wait for Syd to come back. In fact, I think he might have even seen him. They were probably going to the ice cream parlor, too. So anyway that was something. But it was really an interesting place to live at that time because, like I said, we were right near CBS. We were within two blocks to walk to CBS and NBA. And we saw, you know, Jack Benny, Wayne Newton when he first started as a kid. So it was a fun place to be. Q. Did the shortages during the War affect you at all? I mean, the gasoline I know.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Oh, yes, because we had to -- and when you worked during the War, when you worked, by the time you got out of work, you had to go and stand in line. And a lot times there was no meat left really, and I remember pineapple was a shortage, canned pineapple, and I love pineapple, and that was always hard to get, canned pineapple, and meat was especially hard to get. You had a coupon box for certain things.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Sugar.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: And sugar, yes.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Right. So were your family or friends in the Service?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: No. One was an asthmatic, and so he was never. And my dad during World War I had flat feet. They wouldn't take him, so I think -- Syd was an only child. But I lost two very close friends that I had gone all through school from third grade all the way up to graduating from high school, two good friends killed in the War. There was three: One from Scottsbluff, and the other two were from where I was from.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Do you remember where they died?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: I know one was in -- they were both in a plane, the planes were hit. It was a sad, sad time. I hope we don't have another one.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Do you remember going to movies that were about the War, movies that were made about various battles, you know, like Bataan with Robert Taylor and so on?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Oh, yeah, right.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: I know those were hard for people that had lost --

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Right, right. Even now I do not care for anything, but I just want something to be funny or a romantic story. Really it is hard to see some of those things that happened.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: When you were at Lockheed, were there any incidents that stand out in your mind, anything funny that happened or unusual?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: No. I just -- I really can't say that -- I mean, there was a lot of camaraderie because of the War, and when I said that people had given coupons to me so I had enough gas to go to Corpus Christi, and you know, those were touching moments because they were giving up some gas, that maybe they could have gone on a drive or something, because we were limited, and there weren't that many buses. Well, they did have street cars in LA, but that was too far away from where we worked out in the valley.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Did you work -- did you personally work with any people of minority groups?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yes. There were some blacks.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: And how were they treated at work?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Well, I don't remember anything being -- well, I don't think anybody was ever rude to them or anything. As far as I know, those people treated us fine, except they didn't let them in the union.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: So to me, that was not very nice. And they were sacrificing their children, too.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Have you visited any memorials or participated in any commemorations of World War II?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: No. Can't say that I have. I get teary-eyed.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: And I have seen certain things on television about things that happened then. I did -- we did go to Pearl Harbor on a trip during our married life. We did go to Hawaii, and we went out there, and you could have heard a pin drop, all the people that were there. It is a very touching memorial.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Because it is right above the Arizona, isn't it?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yes, it is. You are right over it.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: And you know down there, there were people probably maybe you might have known some of them, too. That was a very touching time to see that.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Did you recycle during the War? You know, it is talking here about rubber and grease, and I remember collecting newspapers, but there was quite a push for recycling certain materials during the War.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yes, there was. And you were supposed to be careful, too, everything you used, you know. But I can't remember it being like it is now because now it is really recycle.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Yes. We waste more now, too.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Well, of course, back then, there were a lot things you couldn't get anyway. They weren't available.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Did we recycle aluminum foil? I know we saved it.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: I don't remember that part because -- well, this is the funny about when I first went to California. We had a studio apartment, four of us. I got there and lived with family friends. The young man was in the Service. Their son was in the Service, and I knew him. We were born in the same town, and he was engaged. So that's who I got this apartment with, was his fiance and her two cousins.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: So we used to laugh because we said we had hot cheeks. We only had one bed, and so can you imagine this happening now days? And we had two worked swing shift, and two worked days. So when they would go to work, we would just be coming home from work. So I can't even imagine now doing this now days, and we would sleep in the same bed that they had slept. I wouldn't no more do that now -- and I know we didn't change the sheets either. But you know, of course, it was very economical that way but still when you stop to think about it.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: You know, they made a movie -- was it Cary Grant and Gene Arthur? They didn't know they were sharing their apartment with somebody else in Washington, D.C. One worked night shift, and the other worked day shift.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yeah. There were we were, two worked swing shift and two-day shift.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Do you remember your address?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: I don't. I don't remember that, but I could go right to it. It was a court, you know, they were all attached, and there was a center where there was grass and so forth. Oh, those were the days, I will tell you. But we also had fun. You had to because of what was going on.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: So living life -- this generation now, I doubt if they would ever do that, share a one-bedroom studio because it had to come out the wall, too. You could imagine.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: A Murphy bed?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yeah. Well, finally, it was getting a little bit much because one of the girls was using my underwear and so forth, and we were supposed to put so much in the little pot for food, too, and so one of the gals and I got our own eventually. So then, that was better, too, than a studio. But there was a shortage then, too, for people that were coming from out of state to help win the War and work in the plants. There was not -- there was quite a housing shortage. Well, and I can remember when we were down in Corpus Christi, Texas, too, that we got a bedroom there because I worked at the base, and it was kitchen privileges.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: How many people did you have to share it with?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Well, there was an older man. He was a salesman, so he wasn't there that much. Then, the lady that had the place was an old grouch. She was always wanting us to get things at the ship's store for her because of things she couldn't get in regular stores. So we would buy her things once in a while, but I remember one time we came up, and she had a note on our mirror and says "please sleep carefully on your sheets," and we wondered now, how do you do that? I never will forget that. So there was a lot of funny things that happened.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Tell me about when you lived in that apartment with the other women, anything interesting or had to do with that time history about makeup and clothes?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Well, first, that's when women started wearing pants, you know, slacks because they were afraid to get -- some of the equipment that you could catch your skirt, you know, and cause a problem, accident of some kind. But that's really when women started wearing slacks. Oh, and that's another thing that was hard to get, were nylons. Well, it wasn't nylons. They were regular silk stockings, and there was a real shortage on women's hosiery. You were lucky to ever get a pair of those.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: So did you use lay makeup?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: So -- yes, yes, uh-huh --

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Did you put the seam up the back?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: -- in the summer. No, I didn't do that. But then, of course, after a while if you went to the beach, it was summer. Of course, it was quite a distance, and it wasn't that easy during the War to go to the beach, but you could lay out in the yard in California and get a tan, and you wouldn't have to lay makeup on. I remember that we used to do that. And a lot of things happened.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Makeup, facial makeup, is cosmetic any different than they are now?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Well, they didn't have the choice. They didn't have the choices that you have now, and it was just sort of standard. I remember Max Factor was the big thing because they had their own plant right there in Hollywood. It wasn't too far from Grauman's Chinese Theater. It is a beautiful building. I think we used to go out and drive around Beverly Hills and see some of the beautiful homes out there. They used to have tours, too, where you could pay, and they would take you and show you who owned which house the stars lived in. So that was a fun thing to do, too. Just having come from Nebraska and seeing a lot of movies, then going out to California and seeing that, it was quite an experience when I was young, you know. That was pretty something. I was the last one -- I had a cousin and my brother, and they both went to California and to Catalina Island. My grandparents used to go out to California every year, and they took my brother to see if he would be better in California with his asthma. And so I always felt like I was the one that didn't get to do all those things. I think that's why I ended up going to California because my brother had been there and so had my cousin, and he was younger than I was, and I think that's one of the reasons I thought I have to get to California.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Well, you were there for a long time?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yeah, I sure was.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Do you remember where you were on V-J Day when you heard that the War was really over?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yes. I think I was going into the hotel in Corpus Christi, Texas. No, that's when the President died.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Oh, that's --

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Roosevelt died.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: And how did you hear about that? What was the reaction?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: It was on the radio, and everybody had a long face when they went into the hotel because they had just heard it, too. So we thought this is the end, you know, the President and the War.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: And it wasn't very long before the V-E Day. He died two or three weeks before V-E Day.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Right, right, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: You knew him. Do you remember where you were then?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: No. I can't say that I do.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Do you remember a celebration after V-J Day?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Oh, yes. Everybody was partying. And I was not a drinker. I never cared much for alcohol.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: But everybody was really dancing in the streets, you know. It was really quite a time.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: What -- you know, this will be seen by people maybe generations from now. Think about what you would like to tell them about experiencing that War and just some thoughts from your point of view.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Well, it was -- thinking this generation now has no idea of what people went through then. I think we had a lot more people that were more dedicated and were hard workers and put in long hours of work. Farmers, of course, farmers still work hard, but in those days there was not all of the mechanical equipment that is available now, and I think, too, there is going to be less and less farms. And it was a of generation hard-working people. And I don't think this generation has any idea as to what people used to go through in those years. So I just -- I always felt lucky. My dad always had a job. And in the depression, a lot of people didn't have jobs, and we didn't have the welfare that we have now.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: What kind work did he do?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: He was a salesman for an independent -- it was called the Donald Company in Grand Island, Nebraska. And they had notions and groceries and their own brands. I remember Rob Roy was the coffee brand, and so -- but he always had a job. But then, in those days when people died, they had no retirement. Social Security hadn't started.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: And that was another thing that was really hard on people. And my dad would never let my mother work. A lot of men didn't let their wives work in those days, but eventually, she had a very good friend that had a -- well, it was a hardware store and crystal and China. And so I guess that's where I got my love of glass, and so she used to go and help out once in a while just as a favor. And she had been a teacher before she married my dad. So it was pretty tough there for a while after he passed away, but she managed. My brother and I helped her, sent so much money home, went to her because, like I said, there was no retirement plans in those days for people.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: And when did your father die, what year approximately?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: 1954 I think it was, something like that. He had an enlarged heart. He had been a smoker, but he was a wonderful man __+.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: So tell me about when you and Syd moved to this area and how long you have lived there.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Oh, we had come up from California to visit our daughter, that an Oregonian had come down there the first day and stayed in California, and in his junior year, he went home and told his mother "I met the girl I am going to marry." Of course, she didn't know that at the time. But anyway so we -- they stayed down there for a few years after he got out school, and then they moved up here. He did not like it down there because they were down there during the Watts Riot. And that was right down in that area, downtown LA. That was bad, and so he never really cared much for Los Angeles. So anyway they moved up here, and then, we had to come up to visit the granddaughter when she was born, and they had another one. Then, we'd come up to visit. We just felt a week at a time was enough. And my husband, he had retired. He worked for the county for 32 years. So he had retirement, and so we used to come up here and visit. We got a vacation house and liked it so much we didn't want to go back. So we bought another house here in Lincoln City and enjoyed. He really enjoyed it because he was born in New York City. He went from New York City to Los Angeles. I didn't know whether he would like a small town or not. That was going to be quite interesting, but he really did because to think he could go to the grocery store or someplace and see somebody he knew, that's so different, and I was used to a small town because I lived in a couple in Nebraska. But now days two people move around so much, and it is because of jobs a lot of times. They promoted or transferred to someplace else. So that's another thing that our generation stayed pretty much put. We lived in the same house for 30 years in California. And of course, that was another wonderful thing when you were a Veteran. They had the GI loans, and this was in a nice part of LA. It was the north part Los Angeles. We could look down and see Catalina Island on a clear day. Well, that didn't last too long because the smog finally entered into it, you know. But we enjoyed coming up here with all the nice fresh air. So we just enjoyed it so much that we ended up staying up here.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: And you moved here permanently?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yeah. He was active in Kiwanis and Preservation at Devil's Lake with the auxiliary as I am and was, and so anyway it has been a nice area. We really enjoyed it.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: So you've lived here about 20 years?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Twenty years we lived here.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: And when did Syd pass away?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: He passed away November 11th, Armistice Day, 2000. He had had Alzheimer's for about six or seven years, and I had to place him. Finally, I couldn't handle it anymore, and so he was in several different places and finally got him in Corvallis. There was no place around here that I felt I cared enough for. Well, they really didn't have any for Alzheimer's people. They were not locked facilities, and so I found a wonderful place in Corvallis, which was ran by Samaritan Hospital, and it was just wonderful. And I went over to see him every week. I think sometimes it was better to have right here near you where you would feel you would have to go everyday, and I know that happened to some people here in town, and I think that's very difficult. So it was -- it is a horrible, horrible thing. I hope they find a cure for that. It is just awful. Of course, they are keeping us living longer now, too, so I think has a lot to do it. But I know somebody over in Beaverton has had it for over 20 years. You know, it is just not fair. It is just sad. Syd would -- ended up by -- he took off several times, and it was like watching a two year-old child.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: I thought I was keeping an eye on him and listening for him and everything. Next thing I knew he was gone. I would have to go out and try and find him. And it is amazing how they are cagey, too, a little cagey. Sometimes you think, oh, they are not too bad, you know. Two minutes later I am off the wall, you know. But it is a horrible thing to go through, and he was always a sweet, gentle, kind man. And when they have Alzheimer's, sometimes they just change, personality and everything.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: The thing that was really interesting to me -- he hadn't known me for several years, but the week that he got ill, and he had been mobile for all this time, but they called and told me he was not eating. Well, Syd loved to eat __+. And I thought something was up, so we went over to see him. And when I went in the room, a friend went with me, but I went in the room, and I laid down and laid a kiss, and he called my name. And that was really tough. My friend that was sitting there behind me, and she said "my God, he said your name," and I think she said that just to reinforce me that I wasn't hearing things. He actually said my name. He knew it was me. So that was -- and he passed away after about an hour-and-a-half.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Well, he had a moment clarity --

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: -- when he saw you.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: That's right. It was really amazing, really amazing. So I miss him.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Yeah, I bet. Did you sing with the Lincoln Pops.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Did you sing with the Lincoln Pops.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: No, I don't. I have had bronchitis so much that I have coughed, you know, and have allergies that I just sound like a gravel garden to me now.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: So you never sang with them?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: No. And I love to sing. We used to have competition, you know, in the different states and districts and so I was sent to the competition of the western regional and our whole state in Nebraska. And I got the highest rating that you can get, but I sure wouldn't make it now, that's for sure. But I do enjoy music.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: You know, you brought a lot news maps they are called and donated them to the museum, and I wondered if you would hold this up, and I will -- they must have been sent to Lockheed every week during the War years, and they have maps and pictures of the progress of the War.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: He was really -- he really enjoyed history, Syd did. His father was born in Poland, and his mother was born in England. His grandmother was born in Russia.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: So I think, you know, those are probably some of the reasons that he __+.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: And I would just scan this, and this one has a map of Philippines and Mendelle, all the Philippine Islands and pictures, a news map, industrial edition. This is a picture of Germany and Belgium down on the corner. And this one came out the week of October 10th to 18th, 1944. The War was winding down.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Roll it back up now?

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Yes. I wish I had a better tripod and wouldn't do all this creeping --

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: You know what? I think I came across -- Syd had so much photography equipment and something like that is folded up, and I am sure it is old, but this one is a lot newer and better than his.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: They have ones what they call floating head, and I just hate to think of it.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: I do, too. Last night on one of the programs -- was it Dateline or 60 minutes -- they interviewed a family that got over here. They were from Iraq. I think the man was a doctor, and so they got out of there. So they feel that he should.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: Yeah. Because they said he just butchered too many people. I don't know. I think there would be another World War and then Korea, too, what's happening there? Now, they said they never had any nuclear weapons.

sp.speaker: Libby Durbin
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Elizabeth Jane Wachs
sp.p: So how do you know? There is always two sides to everything. Well, Libby if you are through with me -- (Interview concluded.)
